title: Ritual 2
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: In this Soto Zen dharma talk, the main teaching emphasizes the transformative power of silence and mindfulness practice. Rather than seeing silence as an absence of sound, it's seen as a positive and powerful experience that allows us to tap into ultimate safety, healing, and peace. By engaging fully with Zazen and participating in rituals like prostrations and incense offerings, we can connect with the Buddha's awakening and cultivate goodness in our lives, ultimately finding freedom from suffering and compassion for ourselves and others.

sentences.text: It's hard to find silence in our world today.
It's a pretty noisy world we live in, and I think that we need silence.
So we're lucky that we can practice silence in this retreat.
Silence isn't the absence of talking or the absence of noise, a kind of negative space or negative virtue born of restraint and some kind of deprivation.
Silence is something strong and positive that emerges right from the middle of sound, because there's always some sound, there's never no sound.
When we quiet the mind, or anyway, better to say, when we stop preventing the mind from coming to quiet, all of a sudden silence springs forth.
Silence is an embracing, intimate experience, and it holds us, brings us a kind of ultimate safety and healing.
Silence is profoundly peaceful, profoundly nurturing, and I think this is why we love nature so much, because nature is so essentially silent.

In the middle of all of nature's wonderful sounds, we hear the voice of silence, which is a much steadier and a much more melodious voice than the usual human chatter that we hear every day in voices and in our own mind.
Silence is not withdrawal.
We're not withdrawing into silence.
Silence is full engagement, maybe the fullest engagement, full engagement at the deepest possible level, beyond the noise of desire and personality.
So try your best to protect and preserve and to practice silence, to allow silence suddenly to spring forward and to allow silence to deepen.
Don't talk.
Don't reach out to others in the usual ways.
Even if there's some sesshin business you need to communicate about, think twice before doing that and see whether it would be just as well to let things go as they are and just return to silence.
In silence, everything is clear and there is no confusion.

Even if the heart-mind is completely confused, it's okay that that be so when you can hear the silence, when you can enter the silence, because the silence heals and encompasses the confusion and eventually brings some peacefulness to it.

I've many times had the experience of being in agitation with my mind full of problems and troubles, and then sitting down right in the middle of that, without trying to solve anything or make anything go away.
After a while, and sometimes it takes a while, my mind does become more quiet, with more equanimity.
So, although it might not always happen like that, silence can also be a problem, and it can always help us.
We're so conditioned to think that we're the ones meditating, that we're going to go and meditate, that we're going to do it well, whoops, we didn't do it so well, we're not doing it so well.
Actually this has never been the case.
We have never been meditating.
Zazen is simply the expression of our willingness to enter silence, of our trust that the silence will awaken us, will help us, will bring some peace to our lives.
A monk asked Zhaozhou, "What about when I'm not chasing after various things?"
Zhaozhou said, "It's just like this."
The monk said, "Isn't this the fact of my own nature?"
And Zhaozhou said, "Chasing, chasing."
So when you're chasing after things in your mind, just practice Zhaozhou's practice here and say to yourself, it's just like this.
Whatever it is, just say, it's just like this.
Apply that phrase, whatever is happening.
If your mind is disturbed, it's just like this.
This is just how it is.
It's just this way.
And when you do that, even though you might not think so, you have stopped chasing after things.
As I was saying yesterday, it's better to think of Zhaozhou as ritual than as some kind of mental or spiritual exercise.
I've been talking to all of you and many other people about practice for a long, long time.
It's been a sobering experience.
We put so much pressure on ourselves.
Somehow, we all imagine that we're supposed to, and we can, solve all of our human problems, achieve enlightenment, get big wisdom, and save the world.
That's what we all think.

And then, when it turns out that the sesshin is over and we've failed at this, apparently, we take it as certain evidence that we have not measured up, that we are, as we always suspected, simply not good enough, not strong enough, not wise enough, not serious enough.
You can fill in your own private, personal ones.
So this is how we are conditioned to look at things, and it's very compelling.
We believe it.
But this is a very foolish setup.
We should be a lot more humble than this.
It's really kind of an arrogant way of looking at things.
The only way that we could think that we're failing is if we have this very high-falutin idea of what we're supposed to be doing.
So we should be a lot more humble.
The truth is, when we are sitting in zazen, we're not trying to do these great things.

We are actually stepping into the ritual of Buddha's awakening, transforming this simple human body born of sperm and egg into the diamond body of Buddha, this confused, conditioned mind into the soaring mind of Buddha.
And we're not doing this symbolically.
We're not doing this metaphorically.
We're actually doing this, whether we know it or not.
I know this because I can tell.
I look around and I see this.
And this is why it makes absolutely no sense to try to be a Buddha.
You see, that trying, that little bit of trying, is the very measure of our confusion.
Of course, we all have to make some effort, but not out of desire to be something that we're not.
We sit, we come back to body and breath over and over again just to do it.
Just because this is our life, this is our humanity, this is our commitment, this is our joy, even if sometimes it's not so much fun.
And it's the enactment of this mysterious ritual of actually stepping into what we really are, whether we know it or not.
It's this enactment, this mysterious ritual, not our skill, not our talent, not our effort, that brings forth the goodness that comes into our lives as a result of our practice.
That's where it comes from.
We have our daily ritual of sitting down in this highly ritualized posture, upright, dignified human posture.
And we are bowing and chanting and offering incense, wearing robes, reenacting the great scenes of the Mahayana sutras of offerings and chanting and so on.
When we repeat these things day after day after day after day, year after year after year, decade after decade, we become them, and they become us.
We become the person who illuminates these practices and the person who is illuminated by them.
And these acts then begin to take on a special weight and power, so that after a while, just to offer one stick of incense, to light one small candle, is to draw forth the whole of the Dharma.
When making prostrations becomes a part of your body, when this becomes the case and you make a prostration, you are literally causing the presence of Buddha to manifest.
This is what brings Buddha alive.
Buddha would be a dead person like a lot of other dead people if it weren't for this re-enlivening of the Buddha that takes place with every prostration.
And we lift the Buddha up with our hands, prostration.

And when we do such things every day in our routine rituals, and it may be that we don't all do them every day, but some of us do on behalf of the others, when we do these things as our ordinary food and drink, we can bring them to the special rituals that we perform less frequently.
Rituals enable expression of human feeling that's there in all of us but wouldn't be expressed or invoked without the space of the ritual.
So, for instance, we can feel a tremendous affection and love for one another.
But if we participate together in a wedding ritual, something changes and the feelings come out in a different way.
In a way the ritual seals the feelings, empowers them differently.
When someone dies, we can express our grief and our joy and our appreciation through a memorial or a funeral ceremony.
That service can be a way of healing and sealing our grief and containing it and expressing it so that it can become a path.
It can become something that we can continuously learn from and develop through because of the ritual.

In these rituals we use sacred words to express the feeling of the occasion, words that are empowered and deepened by the incense, by the prostrations, by the robes, by the monastic deportment, all of which have powerful roots in the long past that one feels at the moment of the ritual.

When we, this year and in the past years, entered Rick and Michael and Kate and John and Tim and Jeff and others as shuso in that simple ritual, it was a chance for us to enact, which we could not have expressed in other ways.

And when later this week we have the Hossen Shiki ceremony, the shuso Hossen Shiki ceremony, the question and answer ceremony, we'll be able to express the Dharma through the forms of that ritual in ways that would be otherwise impossible.

When we go up to Salt Spring after sesshin, many of us together, and we have Jukai ceremony there, we will be able through the ancient form of that ritual to feel the depth and mystery of our commitment to Dharma in a newly empowered way, and it will make a difference and we'll feel different as a result of this.
None of these rituals take too long, and although when you first do them they might seem really complicated, actually they're not so complicated.
But there's a very long route in the past to them, and this route from the past thickens time until the present moment becomes a timeless moment.
It's this timeless moment that is the essence of all ritual, and it's the essence of our sitting practice, if you just look and see.
Another thing about rituals is that mostly we practice them together.
There could be private rituals, but mostly rituals are a chance for us to come together, to unify our hearts, to express a feeling.
And in the ritual of a sesshin, it's not that there are several of us together practicing meditation, each one of us on our own.
It's that all of us are creating this ritual as we practice together as one.

Eating together, bowing, chanting, standing, sitting, walking, lying down in the same space at the same time, and through all these activities, each of us can find the ground of our own mind, the source of our own suffering, and simultaneously the place of our healing, which always involves the recognition that it is actually impossible for any of us ever to be alone and isolated.

Our very problems and sorrows are in their own nature shared problems and sorrows, the same problems and sorrows of all of us throughout time, so that even in the midst of our sorrow or grief or anguish, compassion arises because we're together in it.
There may still be tears, but tears are okay.
Tears can be pretty good.
These are not the tears of anguish.
They're the tears of belonging, the tears of a shared sadness, which is also something very beautiful.
A monk asked Joshua one time, Zhaozhou, "When difficulties come upon us, how can we avoid them?"
And Zhaozhou said something like, "Welcome," something like that.
Recently I was studying again a sutra I've studied many, many times, the mindfulness sutra.

This sutra says that there are four foundations for our mindfulness: kaya, the body; vedana, the feelings; citta, thoughts, emotions, which in Buddhism there's no difference really, it's more or less the same thing, thoughts, emotions, just like heart-mind is the same thing; and dhamma, phenomena.

If you think about what the sutra is saying, it's quite opposed to our Cartesian, Western way of thinking, in which the body has nothing to do with the mind, the mind has nothing to do with the heart.
It's the intellect that counts, which is connected to the spirit.
The emotions and the body have nothing to do with it.
Quite contrary to that, the mindfulness sutra says that you begin with the body, with strong awareness of the body.

When you are deeply with the body, in the body, as the sutra says, and this includes the breath, the body and the breath are one thing, when you can be with the body and the breath, and with all the sensations in the various postures of the body, and also when through this observation you become aware of the impermanent nature of the body, and its flowing, ongoing process, then through this practice of awareness of the body, naturally you will become aware of the deep, unconscious, reactive, emotional setup that is our human, shared human heritage.
And when you feel that in the body, then you will be able to be with the thoughts and emotions without being compelled and dominated by them.
Even though they'll be there, you don't need to be compelled and dominated by them.

And then through this process of allowing what's inside of us to come forth within this field of powerful awareness, just allowing it, not doing anything with it, but just allowing it to arise and pass away within the awareness, we will come to be one with the underlying human pattern that shapes us all.
And then we will have a true measure of freedom and peace.

So, just as Master Zhaozhou says in his beautifully simple way, when difficulties arise, the first thing we want to do, it's just so much who we are, all of us, is get out of there, get rid of those things.
How are we going to do that?
The body just wants to get rid of that right away.
How do we get rid of it?
We get rid of it by being willing not to get rid of it, because it's impossible to get rid of it.
When something is there, it's there.
How is it not going to be there when it's there?
It's there.
And the efforts to make it go away and get rid of it only make it come again.
So the way to get rid of our difficulties is to embrace them.
Welcome.
Okay.
Hello.
If you're here, you might as well come in for a second.
We allow what's there to be there, since it's there, and we're honest about what's there.
We don't pretty it up.
It's liberating to realize how rotten we all are.
It's great.
How exhausting to be good, all the time.
This is really tiring.
Liberating to know what's there.
Still, difficulties are difficulties.
That's why we call them difficulties.
In other words, they're not pleasant, and maybe naturally we're wishing things could be different.
And yet the path to wisdom is through, not around, the difficulties.
So hats off to difficulties.
Thank you, difficulties, because it's through the difficulties that we come to know our humanity.
So our practice is the practice of the mindfulness sutra.
This is exactly what we're doing, exactly as the sutra says.
We establish strong, continuous awareness with the body and the body, with the breath and the breath.
We sit up straight in the natural posture, expressing our utmost human dignity, and we open up our heart-mind fully attentive and welcoming to whatever comes.
We're always coming back over and over again to the body and the breath.
So there's focus.
It's not that we're just flying here and there all the time on our cushions.
There's focus.
But the focus is not a focus.
So whatever comes, we recognize, we greet, we appreciate, we open up our hand and let go.
We come back to presence, come back to the body, come back to the reality, the actual feeling of being in time, which is life.
So the feeling of our practice is at once determined and strong, but at the same time very gentle and permissive.
We don't indulge ourselves in our emotions, but we're also not strict.
We're not trying to push things aside.
And this is not a matter of finding a balance or a compromise between two extremes.
We're not trying to strike a middle.
This is just a matter of being completely present, always, for the new and unexpected moment that will arise if we will allow it.
Whoever you think you are, whatever you think your problems are that keep coming back and back and back over and over again, I wouldn't be too sure about any of that.
Very often, after being quite convinced for 10 or 20 or 30 or 40 years that things are a particular way, all of a sudden you see that actually they're quite different.
They never were that way at all.
People have told me this.
I've heard people tell me this: "All along I thought I was like this, and it turns out that I'm actually like that.
I'm so surprised.
For 30 years I was pretty convinced I was this way, and then I started meditating and I found out that I wasn't."
Sometimes it turns out that deep problems you were positive you had, you actually never did have.
You just were confused about it.
And other problems that you never knew you had suddenly appear to have been there all along, masked by the fake problems that you had thought you had all that time.
And maybe sometimes you sit there and there are no problems at all.
There's nobody there to have any problems.
There's just a kind of very quiet delight that there's anything there at all.
Why should there be?
Who ordained that that would be the case?
But there it is.
A breath, a sound, a little tiny thought feeling floating across the mind's sky.
So this is just to say the ritual of zazen with full openness.
Don't be too sure about anything.
And be ready at all points to start your life over again absolutely fresh.
Be appropriately suspicious of every thought and feeling, but appreciate everything that comes.
Every thought that arises in your mind at this moment, it had to be there.
The entire karma of all the worlds has conspired to bring this thought to you at this time.
Why would you want to complain?
And how could you resist?
So appreciate it.
After all, we can all admire a tricky fellow.
We can admire the trickiness.
As long as we're not hurt, as long as we can see through the trickiness, we can admire it.
A monk once asked Zhaozhou, "What is zazen?"
And Zhaozhou said, "It's non-zazen."
The monk said, "How can zazen be non-zazen?
Does that make any sense?"
And Zhaozhou said, "It's alive."
So that's how we practice.
We're not doing anything.
We're just being alive.
In this spirit, please continue carefully and with full commitment moment after moment, and let's see what happens next.
*May our intention equally penetrate every being and place with the true merit of the Buddha.*
